title: Pre-Mortem Analysis
subtitle: Imagine it already failed then figure out why
useWhen: You are about to launch something, make a major hire, or commit significant resources and you want to stress-test it before you commit. But your team is optimistic and no one is raising the hard questions.
howToUse: The Pre-Mortem was developed by psychologist Gary Klein as an antidote to groupthink and planning optimism. Before a project begins, the team imagines it is one year in the future and the project has failed spectacularly. Each person writes down every reason they can think of for why it failed. The group then reviews all reasons and identifies the most likely and most serious failure modes. Unlike a risk register (which asks 'what could go wrong?'), the Pre-Mortem asks 'what did go wrong?' the past tense activates a different and more honest mode of thinking.
steps: Run the Pre-Mortem in writing first, verbal Pre-Mortems are dominated by the loudest voice.
Separate generation from evaluation, collect all failure reasons before discussing any of them.
Focus on the top 3 most likely and most serious failure modes, you cannot mitigate everything.

For each top failure mode, assign a specific owner and a specific prevention action. A pre-mortem that stays a discussion is wasted effort. If the top three failure modes don't end with a named owner and a specific prevention action, you've identified the risks and done nothing to stop them.
promptBody:
Act as a Pre-Mortem facilitator.
Project or decision      :  [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU ARE ABOUT TO DO]
Timeline                        :  [HOW LONG THIS WILL TAKE]
Team involved              :  [ROLES RESPONSIBLE FOR EXECUTION]
Resources committed :  [BUDGET, TIME, PEOPLE]
Run a Pre-Mortem:
SCENARIO: It is [DATE 12 MONTHS FROM NOW]. This project has failed. Not partially,
completely. What happened?
Generate 10 specific reasons it failed, across:
Execution failures (team, timeline, quality)
Market failures (wrong assumptions about customers)
Resource failures (budget, capacity, dependencies)
Strategic failures (wrong direction or timing)
External failures (competition, regulation, market shift)
Then: rank the top 3 by likelihood × severity.
For each top failure: one prevention action and one owner.

proTip:
The Pre-Mortem's greatest value is not the list of failure modes — it is the social
permission it creates for people to raise concerns. In a team that is committed to a plan,
raising doubts feels disloyal. The Pre-Mortem makes it the job. Run it before every
significant commitment and watch concerns surface that would have stayed silent until
they became problems.
